summary: Henry Herbert Dodwell was a scholar of Indology and history who studied at Lord Williams's School and St John's College, Oxford. He served in the Indian Education Service (1908–1922) and was Professor of History at SOAS (1922–1946).

Henry M. Hoenigswald was a linguist who studied at the universities of Munich, Zurich, Padua, and Florence. He taught Ernest Bender and held a long-term post at the University of Pennsylvania from circa 1948 to 1985.
Henry Martyn worked in linguistics and religious studies. He studied at Truro Cathedral School, graduated from St John's College (circa 1797–1801), and studied under John Borthwick Gilchrist.
Henry Miers Elliot worked in Indology and history and archaeology. Educated at Winchester College, he served as a civil servant for the East India Company from circa 1826 until 1853.

Henry Pitts Forster was an Indologist and linguist who served in the East India Company's Bengal Civil Service from circa 1783 to 1815. He was appointed Master of the Calcutta Mint at the India Government Mint in 1803.

Henry Rawlinson worked in Iranian and Central Asian studies, history, and linguistics after attending Great Ealing School and Middlesex University. He served the East India Company, the Foreign Office, and presided over the Royal Geographical Society and Royal Asiatic Society.
Henry Steel Olcott was a scholar in religious and Buddhist studies who attended Columbia University. In 1875, he co-founded the Theosophical Society.

Henry Sullivan Jarrett worked in history, archaeology, and Indology. Succeeding Heinrich Blochmann, he served as Secretary and Member of the Board of Examiners at Fort William from circa 1870 to 1892.

Henry Thomas Colebrooke was an Indologist who studied under Citrapati. He held civil, judicial, and academic posts with the East India Company, Sadar Diwani Adalat, and Fort William College, and served as Director of the Royal Asiatic Society.
Heramba Chandra Chackravarty was an Indologist who studied under Manindra Mohan Bose. He served as a Lecturer at City College, Kolkata (attested 1977).

Herbert Cushing Tolman was a scholar in linguistics, Indology, and Iranian studies who earned degrees from Yale, Peabody College, Nashville, Hobart, and Louisville. He taught at Yale, Wisconsin-Madison, North Carolina, and Vanderbilt University (1894–1923).

Herbert Franke studied Sinology and Asian history at Bonn, Berlin, and Cologne under Erich Haenisch and Erich Hauer. He served as Professor at the University of Munich (1952–1979) and President of the Bavarian Academy of Sciences and Humanities (circa 1980–1985).
Herbert Hope Risley worked in Indology, history, and archaeology. He received his education at Winchester College (circa 1864–1869) and New College (circa 1869–1873).

Herbert Härtel was an Indologist and historian who studied at Halle and Göttingen under Ernst Waldschmidt. He directed the Museum of Asian Art and held professorships at the University of Berlin and Free University of Berlin.

Herbert Niel Randle was an Indologist and philosopher. He taught philosophy at Sampurnanand Sanskrit University (circa 1908–1927) and served as Librarian of the India Office Library from 1927 to 1949.

Herbert V. Günther studied Buddhist studies and Tibetology at Munich and Vienna under Wilhelm Geiger. He taught at Vienna, Lucknow, and Sampurnanand Sanskrit University before heading the Far Eastern Studies department at the University of Saskatchewan (1964–1984).

Herbert Weir Smyth was a classicist and linguist educated at Swarthmore, Harvard, Leipzig, and Göttingen under Hermann Sauppe. He held academic appointments at Williams College, Johns Hopkins, Bryn Mawr, and Harvard University as Eliot Professor of Greek Literature.

Herman Kellgren was a Finnish scholar of linguistics and Indology who studied under Hermann Brockhaus, Eugène Burnouf, and Philippe Édouard Foucaux. He held an academic post at the University of Helsinki from circa 1849 until 1856.
Herman Wirth studied at Utrecht University from circa 1904 to 1906 and worked in history and archaeology. He held a post at the University of Bern (circa 1909–1910) and founded the Ahnenerbe.

Hermann Beckh was a scholar of Indology, Tibetology, and Buddhist studies who studied at Kiel and the University of Berlin. He held posts at the University of Berlin, the Prussian State Library, and the Kiel Institute for the World Economy.
